_meta: Three variables A, B, C measured over the same five units, constructed so that A correlates strongly and positively with B, B correlates strongly and positively with C, and yet A correlates negatively with C -- a demonstration that correlation is not transitive. The intuition that a positive A-B relationship and a positive B-C relationship force a positive A-C relationship is false: correlation measures the alignment of two variables' deviations, and A can align with B while C aligns with B along a partly opposing direction, so that A and C end up pulling against each other even though both track B. There is a precise mathematical rule behind this: given correlations r(A,B) and r(B,C), the correlation r(A,C) is not fixed but confined to an interval, r(A,C) between r(A,B)*r(B,C) minus sqrt((1-r(A,B)^2)(1-r(B,C)^2)) and r(A,B)*r(B,C) plus that same square-root term. When r(A,B) and r(B,C) are only moderately strong, that lower bound is negative, so a negative r(A,C) is not a paradox but an allowed outcome. These vectors are built as A = B + d and C = B - d for a vector d orthogonal to B, which places r(A,C) exactly at the theoretical minimum of that interval -- the most negative it can be for the given pair of correlations. a, b, c are the three variables' values over the five units. They are the fixture; the three pairwise Pearson correlations, the transitive interval for r(A,C), and where the fixture lands in it are computed.
